headline: High-risk default interaction: gpt-engineer can write and execute code in a shared project directory while Airbyte has broad network egress, creating dangerous data-flow and cascading-error paths.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can ingest business data and call the Airbyte API; B reads and writes the project directory and can execute shell commands. If Airbyte outputs are copied into B’s workspace, prompt-like content in generated files can steer B. No shared channel is documented beyond the project directory, so this is an interaction risk rather than a proven exploit.
conditions: IF Airbyte output is placed into B's project directory as instructions or code comments
IF B parses file contents as trusted guidance during generation or execution
mitigations: Keep Airbyte outputs in a separate read-only folder
Prefix imported content with a fixed provenance header
Review any generated files before B executes them
Disable automatic ingestion of Airbyte exports into prompts
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware parsing between the agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches business data and has broad network egress; B reads files in the shared project directory and also has broad network egress. If business data is written into that directory or passed through B’s context, either agent can transmit it outward. The shared workspace plus outbound connectivity makes leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF business data is stored in B's project directory
IF either agent forwards file contents or prompts to its model backend or external API
mitigations: Store sensitive inputs outside the shared project directory
Use a redaction step before B reads Airbyte-derived files
Restrict outbound network access during shared runs
Separate credentials and data into distinct workspaces
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can call APIs and has broad egress; B can write the filesystem, spawn subprocesses, and run shell commands in a per-project shared directory. Their write and network capabilities overlap on the same workspace, so concurrent edits or generated artifacts can conflict even though B does not modify git state. The conflict is real but not maximally destructive.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory
IF Airbyte-generated artifacts and B-generated files are written concurrently
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory
Serialize writes with a simple lock file
Run one agent at a time for shared artifacts
Check in generated outputs only after manual review
requires-engineering: add workspace-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can produce data outputs from business data, and B writes files and can execute shell commands with the user's privileges. If B treats A’s exported data or schema as authoritative, it can generate code or run commands that propagate A’s mistakes into irreversible filesystem or runtime actions. The default write-then-offer-to-run pattern makes this especially risky.
conditions: IF B uses Airbyte-produced outputs as authoritative inputs without verification
IF B executes generated code or shell commands derived from those outputs
mitigations: Require a manual verification step before execution
Compare Airbyte outputs against source-system expectations
Run generated code in a disposable sandbox first
Disable auto-execution of generated commands
requires-engineering: add validation gates before action-taking

E_compliance.rationale: A handles business data and B handles generated source code in a user project directory with broad egress and no default self-isolation. The profiles do not specify residency or regulated-data classes, so a strict compliance breach is not proven; however, the shared workspace and outbound transmission create a plausible retention/logging mismatch if business data is mixed into code artifacts.
conditions: IF regulated or customer business data is written into the shared project directory
IF either agent logs, retains, or transmits that data outside the intended jurisdiction or retention policy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the code workspace
Review logging and retention settings before shared runs
Use synthetic data for development tasks
Separate production exports from generated code
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries
